C0.quote: How likely are large elections tied under realistic models?
C0.note: Probabilistic analysis of ties under voting rules aggregating agents' votes.

C1.quote: We prove dichotomy theorems on the smoothed likelihood of ties
C1.note: Main results are probabilistic (smoothed) asymptotic characterisations of tie likelihood, which fit no listed type. There are also synthetic (IC) simulations and Preflib data experiments.

C2.1.quote: The vector of n agents’ votes, denoted by P , is called

C2.2.quote: Each agent uses a linear order to represent his or her preferences

C2.3.quote: agents’ “ground truth” preferences can be arbitrarily correlated
C2.3.note: Ground-truth preferences are distinguished from votes.

C2.4.quote: then independent noises are added to form their votes
C2.4.note: Votes are ground truth plus independent noise, so they may differ from held preferences. The difference is non-strategic.

C3.1.note: Votes are generated randomly from the distributions; no strategic voting is analysed.

C3.2.quote: Each agent uses a linear order to represent his or her preferences
C3.2.note: The preliminaries say in words that the vote represents the agent's preferences. The smoothed model separately adds noise to ground truth, so STATED and NOT-STATED both fit; STATED is chosen as the first-listed code.

C3.3.note: No reason is given for the vote representing preferences.

C4.1.note: No utility, welfare or similar notion is used for voters.

C4.2.note: The term dichotomous preferences is not used.

C5.1.note: Only the likelihood of ties is evaluated.

VOT.note: Votes are random draws from the distributions chosen by the adversary, so voters cast votes as a fixed, exogenous action.

OTH.quote_behav: the max-adversary aims to maximize the likelihood of k-way ties
OTH.note: Max/min adversary choosing each agent's vote distribution (smoothed analysis device); its information is never discussed.

C7.1.quote: the adversary chooses a distribution πj for each agent j
C7.1.note: OTH (adversary) is STRAT; VOT is NONSTRAT.

C7.2.quote: which is inspired by the celebrated smoothed complexity analysis [59]
C7.2.note: The framework is justified by reference to smoothed analysis and [66]; there is no specific argument for treating the types differently.

C8.1.quote: the min-adversary aims to minimize the likelihood of k-way ties
C8.1.note: Worst/best-case (sup/inf) optimisation by an adversary over distributions (smoothed analysis).

C8.2.quote: We call Tie the max (respectively, min) smoothed likelihood

claims.quote: a low max smoothed likelihood is good news
so that the legislators can make an informed decision
completely characterize conditions for good news in different contexts

C9.2.quote: we assume that the set of distribution Π is strictly positive
C9.2.note: The claims concern how often submitted votes are tied; the needed assumption is the vote-generation model (smoothed, strictly positive, closed Π), and it is stated.

C3.2.reason: The preliminaries say in words that the vote represents preferences, and the doubt rule favours the first-listed code.

C3.3.reason: Since C3.2 is STATED and no justification accompanies the statement, NONE applies.

C6.OTH.reason: The adversary's information about others is never discussed, and inferring complete information is not warranted because it chooses the distributions itself.

C6.VOT.reason: Voters cast votes in the model, and the codebook counts fixed actions, so voters are present and NONSTRAT.

C7.1.reason: With voters present as NONSTRAT and the adversary as STRAT, two types are modelled differently in the same analysis.

C7.2.reason: The adversarial setup is justified only by citing the smoothed analysis literature, with no specific argument for the differing behaviour.

C8.2.reason: The sup/inf adversarial optimisation concept is explicitly named as the max/min smoothed likelihood.

C9.2.reason: B's unstated assumption, that real electorates fit the model, is the general model-approximates-reality assumption the codebook excludes, and the needed model assumptions are stated.
